newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Britain puts out bunting for queen's golden wedding.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Britain puts out bunting for queen's golden wedding.

text.p: China mug factories are cranking up production, garden party guests are busy buying new hats and the royal family's glass coach is getting an unscheduled outing from Buckingham Palace.
Britain is putting out its royal bunting for Queen Elizabeth's golden wedding anniversary with an enthusiasm unseen since the 1981 fairytale wedding of Prince Charles and Princess Diana.
That marriage's nightmarish end soured the nation's love affair with its monarchy and only Elizabeth, the 96-year-old Queen Mother, was untouched by the public's disdain.

But in stark contrast to the lack of fanfare when the queen turned 70 in April last year, Britons are marking her 50 years of marriage to Prince Philip with lavish spectacles and affectionate tribute.

The anniversary itself does not fall until November 20, when a Thanksgiving Service is being held in Westminster Abbey and the government and the Lord Mayor of London host official dinners and lunches for the couple.
But the celebrations kick off next week with a pageant which organisers say will be the biggest equestrian event ever staged.

More than 1,300 horses and 4,000 men, women and children will relate the history of the horse and how it has helped man through peace, war, work and sport in a live open-air show performed in front of the horse-loving royal family and a 23,000-strong audience at Windsor Great Park, outside London.

Highlights of the 2.5 million pound ($4.2 million) spectacle -- all of which is privately funded -- will include a re-enactment of the 1854 Charge of the Light Brigade, complete with cannons, and the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse brandishing swinging skulls and wearing metal-framed costumes up to 15 feet (4.6 Metres) high.

The finale will see the departure of the queen and Prince Philip in the same magnificent glass stagecoach in which they left Westminster Abbey 50 years ago in a lavish ceremony that signalled Britain's emergence from the dark days of World War Two.

"I thought it would be rather nice to do the biggest and most complicated horse show in the world. If it's not a challenge, there's no point. It's got to be better than anything I've done before," said Major Michael Parker, whose previous spectacles have included the 1995 VE Day celebrations.
ROYALS LOVE OF HORSES
The prospect of hundreds of amateurs dressing up in fancy costumes and racing around on horses might seem bizarre to anyone other than the English upper classes.

But there could be few subjects closer to the hearts of both the queen and her husband than horses. She is a successful breeder as well as an owner of race horses, and he is keen on polo and carriage driving.
It's a passion the royal couple have passed on to their children -- Prince Charles plays polo and Princess Anne rode for Britain in the 1976 Olympics.
Charles, Anne and Prince Andrew have all divorced and the acrimony and scandal surrounding the break-ups risked turning the monarchy from an object of respect into one of ridicule.

Such was the plunging popularity of the royal family two years ago that Waterford Wedgwood, makers of royal memorabilia china for more than 230 years, at first decided against making a special golden wedding mug for the queen.
But it reversed the decision last month after bowing to popular demand, and is now working flat out to get commemorative items ready for the shops.
The Royal Mint is striking a special gold coin showing the queen and Prince Philip face to face, and Aynsley China is rolling out the cups, mugs and commemorative plates.
"It is no secret that the royals have undergone a change in people's respect. But we haven't seen a change as we attract the staunch royalists," said Ken Barnes of Aynsley China.

Four thousand British couples, some of them expatriates, who also married in 1947, are attending a special Buckingham Palace garden party on July 15 -- an event set up by the queen herself and for which tickets were 10 times over-subscribed.

The days of nationwide street parties that marked the royal golden years of the 1970s and 1980s have ended, along with the tax-free status and the royal yacht enjoyed by the monarch, when wealth and privilege went unquestioned.
But the queen appears to have weathered the storms of the past 10 years and emerged fitter, leaner and ready to sail into the 21st century.
A royal web site launched on the Internet by Buckingham Palace in March is attracting up to one million hits a day from the curious and the loyal all over the world.
The 250-page web site includes a "visitors' book", where surfers on the information super highway can leave their comments about the royal family.
"The vast majority are supportive, which is a morale-booster," said a Buckingham Palace spokeswoman. ($ = 0.600 British Pounds)
